source.title: Context parroting: A simple but tough-to-beat baseline for foundation models in scientific machine learning

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neural scaling laws and tests a different relationship: forecasting error and motif distance versus context length for context parroting on time-series data. It does not test held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute, compute-optimal allocation, or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites general neural scaling laws and reports a context-length scaling result for context parroting. That result is recorded under fits_no_version because it concerns a different resource and measure from the claim. Results comparing forecast models, attractor metrics, and inference costs do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study's scaling results concern forecast error versus context length for a non-neural context-parroting algorithm on chaotic time series. It does not measure pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute, compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape, or downstream performance versus model scale. Foundation-model comparisons are performance benchmarks at fixed sizes and do not bear on any version. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The main conclusion is that context parroting beats leading time-series foundation models on chaotic and other SciML forecasting tasks at negligible cost, which exposes their failure modes. Secondarily, parroting reproduces an in-context power law in context length, with exponent linked to the attractor's correlation dimension. The record's paraphrase understates the main benchmark conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies context-length scaling for a time-series forecasting algorithm, rather than pretraining-loss scaling across model size, data, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: For context parroting, the paper reports power-law scaling across embedding dimensions D = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30; it also reports that the exponent varies by chaotic system and is related to correlation dimension.

fits_no_version.finding: For context parroting on 135 dysts chaotic systems, one-step sMAPE and nearest-motif distance fall as power laws in context length for D=5 to 30 (Fig. 10). In Fig. 5 they share a common exponent α.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context scaling: forecast error of nearest-neighbour copying falls as a power law in context length.

fits_no_version.finding: Exponent α tracks inverse attractor correlation dimension (theory α=1/dcor; Spearman around 0.85, D=10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The context-length scaling exponent is set by the data's intrinsic (fractal) dimension.

record.problems: The paper's scaling results concern context length and time-series forecasting, not the claim's pretraining-loss, parameter, token, compute, or allocation relationships. The scaling plots do not give numerical fit exponents or uncertainty bounds in the provided text.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-bearing result rows were left out. Other forecasting comparisons and metrics were excluded because they do not measure the scaling relationships named in the claim versions.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; not studied.
Extrapolation from small to large training runs; not studied.
Depth/width effects at fixed parameter count; not studied.
Pretraining-resource scaling in other modalities or regimes. The context-length power law is for an inference-time algorithm, not training-resource scaling.
Downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss; not studied.
Dependence of LM exponents or allocation on setup or fitting choices; not studied.

record.verdict_notes: R13 states the correlation between dcor and 1/α, and the reported figure plots α versus 1/dcor. Either way it is a context-length result. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. Context length is an inference resource, not a training resource, so V5 does not apply.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, and training compute.
Whether fits from small language-model pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including how either scales with training compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on language-model pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
Whether the claimed pretraining scaling law transfers to other modalities or training regimes. The paper studies context-length scaling in time-series forecasting, not pretraining-resource scaling.
Downstream performance as a function of language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of the specified language-model exponents and compute-optimal allocation on setup or fitting choices.
